Heraclitus. Around five hundred and thirty-five to four hundred and seventy-five BCE. He was an Ionian Greek philosopher known for the doctrine of universal flux—that all things are in constant change. He believed that a unifying rational principle, which he called the logos, governs reality. His aphoristic, paradoxical style and emphasis on tension and opposition made him a defining voice in pre-Socratic philosophy and a direct foil for Parmenides.

Heraclitus was born in Ephesus, a wealthy Ionian city. He lived a reclusive life of contemplation. He wrote a single work, which became known as the logos, but it is now lost. What survives are fragments quoted by later philosophers. He expressed his ideas in cryptic, aphoristic statements and riddles. He earned the nickname "the Obscure" for this deliberately obscure style, which he meant to exclude the vulgar and reward careful thought.

His core claim was that everything flows. Panta rhei. The world is in constant flux and motion. He said you cannot step into the same river twice. Change is so radical that neither the river nor you are the same from moment to moment. Fire, he argued, is the primal element. It symbolizes change, transformation, and the dynamic nature of reality. Opposition and tension are not static. They are dynamic—things held in unity through perpetual opposition.

Yet within this constant change, reality is governed by a rational principle he called the logos. It is an order and rationality that pervades all things. Humans are separated from this logos by ignorance and sleep. Philosophy awakens us to its truth. The logos is divine and immanent, not transcendent. Though all things change, the logos itself—the principle of change—remains eternal and unchanging.

This put Heraclitus in direct opposition to Parmenides. Parmenides later argued for unchanging Being. Heraclitus prioritized becoming. This opposition between flux and permanence defined a central tension in Western metaphysics. Hegel revived Heraclitus enthusiastically, seeing dialectical opposition as Heraclitean flux. His aphoristic, paradoxical style made him the poet-philosopher, and it influenced how later philosophers use language to provoke insight.
